shots.vo: What if tomorrow, it started raining *glass*?
Not hail. Hair-thin threads of glass — they really fall in Hawaii during eruptions. They're called *Pele's hair*.
A thread can be longer than three feet and *thinner than a millimeter*. It cuts skin, eyes and lungs.
People run down the street, *covering their faces*.
The sky closes to planes. Volcanic ash is rock and glass, and the glass *melts inside jet engines*.
In nineteen eighty-two, a Boeing seven forty-seven flew into ash, and *all four engines* died.
The captain said: "We have a small problem. *All four engines have stopped*."
The plane fell for four miles before the engines came back. *All two hundred sixty-three* people survived.
Now the glass is over the whole planet. *Not a single flight* takes off.
People unhook their gutters, or the glass ends up in *drinking water*.
Cows and sheep eat grass along with the glass. It *won't wash off*.
Farms empty out. *So do store shelves*.
It has happened before: in eighteen fifteen, the Tambora volcano blasted *billions of tons* of ash and gas into the sky.
The next year was called *the Year Without a Summer*. It snowed in June in America, crops died, and famine followed.
Glass barely breaks down. In nature it takes *a million years* or more.
Beaches, fields, parks — all covered in glass for *thousands of generations*.
So if it rains tomorrow, be glad it's *just water*.
